plan: Complete enhanced-ACT humanities passage (CLD-P-ACT-R-000042, 'Second Thoughts in Paint'), about 620 words, on pentimenti: the Dresden Vermeer restoration (Cupid revealed, later overpaint removed in 2021), Picasso's Old Guitarist, X-ray and infrared imaging, what pentimenti show historians, and the restoration debate. Topic checked against all ACT Reading passages (no art-restoration passage; the SAT R&W bank has an unrelated underdrawing item). 10 questions.

passages.title: Second Thoughts in Paint
passages.text:
When conservators at the Old Masters Picture Gallery in Dresden began cleaning Johannes Vermeer's Girl Reading a Letter at an Open Window in 2017, they expected mainly to remove centuries of yellowed varnish. They already knew, from X-ray images made decades earlier, that a large painting of Cupid, the god of love, lay hidden beneath a stretch of plain wall behind the young woman, and scholars had long assumed that Vermeer himself painted over it, having changed his mind about what the room should contain. But when the conservators analyzed the layers of paint, they found that the covering had been added well after Vermeer's death. Someone else had hidden the Cupid. After much debate, the museum removed the later paint, and in 2021 the picture went back on display with Cupid restored.

The Dresden case is unusual, but the kind of hidden layer that started the story is not. Painters have always changed their minds, and traces of those changes often survive beneath the finished surface. Art historians call such traces pentimenti, from an Italian word meaning "repentances." A few become visible to the naked eye as the upper layers of oil paint grow more transparent with age: in Pablo Picasso's The Old Guitarist, painted in the early 1900s, the faint outline of a woman's head can be seen near the guitarist's neck. Most, however, are found with tools that see below the surface. X-rays pick up dense pigments such as lead white, and infrared cameras can reveal sketches drawn on the canvas before any paint was applied.

For historians, pentimenti offer something that finished paintings rarely do: a record of decisions. A shifted arm, a hand painted in two positions, a window that was once a door—each shows that the composition we see was not the only one the artist considered. Studying such changes, scholars can sometimes tell an original from a copy, since a copyist who already knows the final image has little reason to try out alternatives. They can also watch an artist working through a problem, rejecting one solution and choosing another.

Yet pentimenti also raise an uncomfortable question about what, exactly, a painting is. If a painting is whatever its artist finally intended, then the Dresden conservators were right to remove a covering added by someone else. But the plain wall had been part of the painting for most of its existence. Generations of viewers had known the work only in that form, and some critics argued that its empty background had become part of the picture's quiet appeal. Removing it, they said, meant trading a painting people had admired for centuries for one that only Vermeer and his first viewers had seen.

No rule settles such disputes. Conservators must weigh the artist's intention against the history of the object itself, and reasonable experts disagree about how to do so. What pentimenti make clear is that a painting is less a single fixed image than a surface that holds many moments at once: the artist's first ideas, second thoughts, and final choices, and sometimes the choices of people who came later.

candidates.stem: Which of the following statements best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Vermeer frequently painted over parts of his own finished work, as X-ray studies of many of his paintings in museums have repeatedly shown.
choices.B: Hidden changes beneath paintings reveal how artists worked and raise hard questions about which version of a painting should be preserved.
choices.C: Modern imaging tools have now made it possible to determine exactly what every artist originally intended to paint.
choices.D: Restorers should always return a painting to its earliest known state, as the Dresden museum correctly did in 2021.

candidates.evidence: What pentimenti make clear is that a painting is less a single fixed image
candidates.explanation: The passage uses the Dresden case and the idea of pentimenti to show both what hidden changes reveal about artists and the restoration questions they raise.

A.rationale: The passage says the Dresden covering was added by someone else after Vermeer's death.

C.rationale: The passage says experts still disagree and that no rule settles such disputes.

D.rationale: The author presents both sides of the Dresden debate and does not endorse a rule.

hints: What two things do pentimenti do, according to paragraphs 3 and 4?

strategy.explanation: Combine the passage's two main points.

candidates.remember: A main idea must cover the passage's central claims without overstating them.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, what did the conservators' analysis of the paint layers show about the plain wall covering the Cupid?

choices.A: It had been painted by Vermeer shortly before his death.
choices.B: It had been added by Vermeer's students while he was still painting.
choices.C: It had been revealed by X-rays only during the 2017 cleaning.
choices.D: It had been added well after Vermeer died.

candidates.evidence: the covering had been added well after Vermeer's death
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 1 states that the covering "had been added well after Vermeer's death."

A.rationale: The analysis showed it was added well after his death.

B.rationale: The passage says only that it was added after his death by someone else.

C.rationale: X-rays had revealed the hidden figure decades earlier.

hints: Find what the analysis of the layers showed.
candidates.remember: Watch for choices that mix real details from the wrong part of the passage.

candidates.stem: The main purpose of the first paragraph is to:

choices.A: present a specific case that introduces both hidden painted layers and the restoration debate discussed later.
choices.B: explain in detail the scientific methods that conservators use to date the separate layers of paint in an old picture.
choices.C: argue that the Dresden museum should have left the painting exactly as visitors had always seen it.
choices.D: compare Vermeer's working methods with those of Pablo Picasso and other painters of later centuries.

candidates.evidence: After much debate, the museum removed the later paint
candidates.explanation: The Dresden story introduces a hidden layer (developed in paragraphs 2–3) and a disputed removal (developed in paragraph 4).

B.rationale: The paragraph mentions an analysis but does not explain how it works.

C.rationale: The paragraph reports the decision without judging it; objections come in paragraph 4.

D.rationale: Picasso is not mentioned until paragraph 2, and no comparison is made.

hints: Which later paragraphs return to the Dresden case?

strategy.explanation: Ask what the opening sets up.

candidates.remember: An opening anecdote often previews several later points.

candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 5, the word "settles" most nearly means:
candidates.explanation: A rule that settles a dispute decides or resolves it.

A.rationale: Although "settle" can mean calm down, the sentence is about disputes being decided.

B.rationale: "Settle" can mean to make a home in a new place, but that does not fit disputes.

D.rationale: Nothing is sinking; the sentence concerns ending disagreements.

hints: What would a rule do to a dispute?

strategy.explanation: Replace the word with your own.

candidates.remember: Choose the meaning that fits the sentence's subject and object.

candidates.stem: Based on paragraph 3, which of the following might scholars suspect about a painting that shows no pentimenti at all?

choices.A: It could be a copy made by someone who already knew the finished image.
choices.B: It must be an original, since copyists usually make many changes.
choices.C: It was made by an artist who never considered other compositions.
choices.D: It has been damaged by too much cleaning over the years.

candidates.evidence: a copyist who already knows the final image has little reason to try out alternatives
candidates.explanation: Because copyists already know the final image, their work tends to lack trial changes; a painting with none might therefore be a copy.

B.rationale: The passage says copyists have little reason to try alternatives, so a lack of changes points the other way.

C.rationale: The passage does not draw this conclusion; it links a lack of changes to copying.

D.rationale: Nothing connects missing pentimenti to cleaning damage.

hints: Who has little reason to try alternatives?

strategy.explanation: Apply the stated reason to the new case.

candidates.remember: Apply a stated cause-and-effect relationship to a new example.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, infrared cameras can reveal:

choices.A: dense pigments such as lead white in the paint.
choices.B: sketches drawn on the canvas before any paint was applied.
choices.C: the exact date when each layer of paint was added.
choices.D: varnish on the surface that has turned yellow with age.

candidates.evidence: infrared cameras can reveal sketches drawn on the canvas before any paint was applied
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 2 says infrared cameras "can reveal sketches drawn on the canvas before any paint was applied."

A.rationale: That is what X-rays pick up.

C.rationale: The passage does not say infrared cameras date layers.

D.rationale: Varnish is mentioned only in the Dresden cleaning, not with infrared cameras.

candidates.remember: When two similar tools are described, match each to its own result.

candidates.stem: In paragraph 3, the examples "a shifted arm, a hand painted in two positions, a window that was once a door" mainly serve to:

choices.A: suggest that most artists painted carelessly and had to correct mistakes.
choices.B: describe the specific changes found beneath the Dresden Vermeer.
choices.C: explain how X-rays distinguish one pigment from another.
choices.D: illustrate the kinds of changes that show an artist considered other compositions.

candidates.evidence: each shows that the composition we see was not the only one the artist considered
candidates.explanation: The list gives concrete instances of pentimenti, and the sentence says each shows the artist considered other compositions.

A.rationale: The examples are presented as decisions, not carelessness.

B.rationale: The Dresden painting's hidden layer was a Cupid; these are general examples.

C.rationale: The examples concern compositional changes, not imaging methods.

hints: What does the rest of the sentence say about the examples?

strategy.explanation: Read the whole sentence containing the list.

candidates.remember: Lists of examples usually illustrate the claim made in the same sentence.

candidates.stem: The critics described in paragraph 4 would most likely agree with which of the following statements?

choices.A: A painting should always be returned to the exact state that its artist finally intended for it.
choices.B: Conservators should not use X-rays or other imaging tools to study the hidden layers of old paintings.
choices.C: How a painting has been seen over its long history should count in deciding what form it should take.
choices.D: Vermeer's original Cupid was poorly painted and not worth the effort of uncovering and displaying.

candidates.evidence: Generations of viewers had known the work only in that form
candidates.explanation: The critics argued that the plain wall had been part of the painting for centuries and had become part of its appeal, so they value the object's history alongside the artist's intention.

A.rationale: The critics opposed removing the later paint, which is what that principle would require.

B.rationale: The critics object to removing the covering, not to studying the painting.

D.rationale: The critics' objection concerns the covering's long history, not the Cupid's quality.

hints: Why did the critics object to removing the wall?

strategy.explanation: State the critics' reason in your own words.

candidates.remember: To infer a viewpoint, generalize from the reasons the group gives.

author_checklist.hardness: Requires generalizing the critics' specific objection into a principle and rejecting the intention-only principle.

candidates.stem: Which example from the passage best supports the author's claim in paragraph 5 that a painting can be "a surface that holds many moments at once"?

choices.A: The Dresden Vermeer described in paragraph 1
choices.B: Picasso's The Old Guitarist, described in paragraph 2
choices.C: The copies that scholars try to identify, described in paragraph 3
choices.D: The examples of changed arms, hands, and windows listed in paragraph 3

candidates.evidence: and sometimes the choices of people who came later
candidates.explanation: The claim includes "the choices of people who came later"; the Dresden painting holds both Vermeer's composition and a later person's covering, so it best illustrates the claim.

B.rationale: Its hidden head reflects only Picasso's own changes; the claim also includes the choices of people who came later.

C.rationale: Copies are described as lacking trial changes, so they hold fewer moments, not many.

D.rationale: These examples show an artist's own changes but not the choices of later people.

hints: Which example includes changes by more than one person?

strategy.explanation: Match every part of the claim.

candidates.remember: The best support matches all parts of a claim, not just one.

author_checklist.hardness: Requires matching the claim's final clause (later people's choices) to the one example that includes them.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, some pentimenti become visible to the naked eye because:

choices.A: conservators remove the top layer of paint during cleaning.
choices.B: artists deliberately leave earlier versions showing.
choices.C: X-rays permanently change the color of lead white.
choices.D: the upper layers of oil paint grow more transparent as they age.

candidates.evidence: as the upper layers of oil paint grow more transparent with age
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 2 says some pentimenti become visible "as the upper layers of oil paint grow more transparent with age."

A.rationale: The passage links visibility to the paint's aging, not to cleaning.

B.rationale: Nothing suggests the earlier versions were left visible on purpose.

C.rationale: X-rays are a viewing tool; the passage does not say they alter paint.

hints: What happens to oil paint over time?
candidates.remember: Cause questions are answered by the reason the passage states.

revision_log.reason: Round-1 blind solves matched every key. Fixes: paragraph 1 implied the Cupid was a surprise although X-rays had shown it decades earlier (reworded); R042-01 choice D and R042-09 choices A/B restated facts tested by R042-02 and R042-10 (rewrote 01 D; 09 choices now name the examples by paragraph instead of restating them); R042-05's stem overstated what scholars would conclude (now 'might scholars suspect'). Whole batch re-solved blind.

Round-2 solves matched every key with no blocking flags; one noted that R042-03 choice C ('paint that was added after Vermeer's death') restated R042-02's answer. Reworded that distractor. Re-solved blind.
